topics.title: Large Language Models
topics.description: Learn how large language models work, how they are trained, and how to use them effectively.

lessons.title: What are Large Language Models?
lessons.body:
# What are Large Language Models?

Large Language Models (LLMs) are neural networks trained on large amounts of text to predict and generate language. Given a sequence of tokens (pieces of words), an LLM estimates which token is most likely to come next.

## Key ideas

- **Tokens**: Text is split into tokens before processing. A token might be a word, part of a word, or punctuation.
- **Training**: During pretraining, the model learns patterns in language by predicting the next token across billions of examples. Later stages (like instruction tuning) help it follow directions and answer questions.
- **Context window**: An LLM can only consider a limited amount of text at once. This limit is called the context window.
- **Probabilistic output**: The model produces probabilities over possible next tokens, so the same prompt can lead to different outputs depending on sampling settings.

## Why it matters

LLMs can summarize text, answer questions, write code, and assist with many language tasks. They are powerful, but they can also make mistakes or produce confident-sounding incorrect answers, so their output should be verified when accuracy matters.

questions.text: What is the core task an LLM is trained to do during pretraining?
questions.explanation: During pretraining, LLMs learn by predicting the next token in a sequence. This objective teaches the model statistical patterns in language across large text corpora.

options.text: Predict the next token in a sequence
Execute programs written by users
Store every document it reads in a database
Verify facts using external sources by default

questions.text: What is a token in the context of LLMs?
questions.explanation: LLMs process text as tokens, which are units such as whole words, subwords, or punctuation. Tokenization converts raw text into the numerical inputs the model can work with.

options.text: A security credential used to access the model API
A unit of text, such as a word or part of a word
A single training example from the dataset

questions.text: What does an LLM's context window describe?
questions.explanation: The context window is the maximum amount of input (and generated) text, measured in tokens, that the model can consider at one time. Information outside that window is not directly available to the model.

options.text: The time it takes to train the model
The number of users who can access the model at once
The amount of text the model can consider at one time
The size of the model's weights on disk

questions.text: Why can the same prompt produce different responses from an LLM?
questions.explanation: LLMs generate outputs by sampling from probability distributions over next tokens. Sampling settings (and inherent randomness in decoding strategies) can lead to different valid continuations for the same prompt.

options.text: Because the model randomly deletes parts of the prompt
Because outputs are sampled from probabilities over possible tokens
Because LLMs always query a live search engine
Because each request retrains the model

questions.text: Which statement best describes a limitation of LLMs?
questions.explanation: LLMs can generate plausible but incorrect information, sometimes called hallucinations. When correctness matters, users should verify important outputs against trusted sources or checks.

options.text: They can produce confident but incorrect answers
They can only process numbers, not text
They cannot generate code in any programming language
They require users to provide model weights with every prompt
They always return the same answer for every question

questions.text: What is a common purpose of instruction tuning after pretraining?
questions.explanation: Instruction tuning trains the model on examples of following instructions and helpful responses. It helps align the pretrained model's behavior with user requests, making it more useful as an assistant.

options.text: To reduce the model's vocabulary to a single language
To help the model follow directions and respond usefully

topics.title: AI Agents
topics.description: Learn what AI agents are, how they use tools and planning, and where human oversight matters.

lessons.title: What is an AI Agent?
lessons.body:
# What is an AI Agent?

An AI agent is a system that uses a model to pursue a goal by choosing actions, often across multiple steps. Unlike a single prompt-response interaction, an agent can observe results, decide what to do next, and continue until it reaches an outcome or stops.

## Core parts

- **Goal**: The task the agent is trying to accomplish, usually provided by a user or system.
- **Reasoning and planning**: The agent breaks work into steps, decides which action is most useful, and adapts when results are unexpected.
- **Tools**: Agents can call external capabilities such as search, code execution, databases, or APIs to gather information or perform actions.
- **Memory/state**: The agent tracks relevant context, intermediate results, and progress.

## Human oversight

Agents can be useful for research, coding, and workflow automation, but they can also take wrong actions or act on incorrect assumptions. Clear permissions, guardrails, and review points are important when actions affect real systems or data.

questions.text: What best distinguishes an AI agent from a single chat response?
questions.explanation: An agent can take multiple steps toward a goal, often using observations and tool results to decide what to do next. A single response does not by itself involve this ongoing action loop.

options.text: It can pursue a goal through multiple actions over time
It never makes mistakes
It only works without any model
It always requires retraining for each task

questions.text: Why might an AI agent use tools?
questions.explanation: Tools let an agent access information or perform actions beyond text generation, such as querying an API, running code, or reading files. This helps the agent complete tasks that require external data or side effects.

options.text: To replace the need for any instructions
To access external capabilities or information needed for a task
To guarantee the answer is always correct

questions.text: What is a sensible safety practice when an agent can change real systems?
questions.explanation: When actions have real impact, permissions and review points reduce risk. Guardrails such as limited tool access, confirmations, and logging help prevent unintended or harmful changes.

options.text: Give it unrestricted access so it works faster
Disable all logging to simplify debugging
Use permissions, guardrails, and human review for impactful actions
Assume tool results are always trustworthy

questions.text: In an agent loop, what typically happens after a tool returns a result?
questions.explanation: Agents use observations, including tool outputs, to update their understanding of the task. They then decide the next step, which may be another tool call, a request for clarification, or a final response.

options.text: The agent ignores the result and restarts training
The agent uses the result to decide the next action
The tool output is automatically published to users
The context window becomes unlimited

questions.text: Which task is a good fit for an agentic approach?
questions.explanation: Agentic systems are useful when a task requires several steps and interaction with external information or tools. Simple, single-step tasks may not need an agent loop.

options.text: A task requiring multiple steps, such as researching and summarizing sources
Returning a fixed string with no decisions
A task where no information or actions are needed
Storing data without any logic or goal
Rendering a static label in a UI

questions.text: What does 'state' or memory help an agent do?
questions.explanation: State helps an agent keep track of what has already happened, such as completed steps, tool results, and remaining work. Without relevant state, multi-step tasks become unreliable.

options.text: Track progress and relevant information across steps
Increase model weights during every request

topics.title: Model Context Protocol
topics.description: Learn how MCP connects AI applications to tools and data sources through a standard interface.

lessons.title: Introduction to MCP
lessons.body:
# Introduction to MCP

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol for connecting AI applications to external tools, data sources, and workflows. Instead of building a custom integration for every model-to-system pair, MCP provides a standard way for clients and servers to exchange capabilities and context.

## How it works

- **MCP host/client**: The AI application (such as an editor assistant or agent runtime) uses an MCP client to discover and call capabilities.
- **MCP server**: A server exposes specific capabilities, such as tools, resources, or prompts, often backed by a local system or remote service.
- **Standard interface**: Because the protocol is consistent, a client can work with many servers without bespoke glue code for each one.

## Why it matters

MCP helps teams reuse integrations, control what an AI system can access, and make tool access more portable. As with any integration, servers should expose only the capabilities needed and handle authentication and permissions carefully.

questions.text: What problem does MCP primarily address?
questions.explanation: MCP standardizes how AI applications connect to external tools and data sources. This reduces the need for one-off integrations between every client and every system.

options.text: Standardizing connections between AI applications and external capabilities
Replacing all databases with language models
Training foundation models faster
Compressing prompts to fewer tokens

questions.text: In MCP, what is the role of an MCP server?
questions.explanation: An MCP server exposes capabilities such as tools, resources, or prompts. A client connects to the server to discover and use those capabilities through the protocol.

options.text: To expose tools or data capabilities through a standard interface
To fine-tune the client model on every request
To prevent the client from using any external data

questions.text: Why is a standard protocol useful for tool integrations?
questions.explanation: A shared protocol lets clients and servers interoperate without custom adapters for each pairing. This improves reuse and makes integrations easier to maintain and swap.

options.text: It means integrations never need authentication
It allows reusable integrations across compatible clients and servers
It guarantees every tool call returns correct data
It removes the need to review permissions

questions.text: Which is an example of a capability an MCP server might provide?
questions.explanation: MCP servers commonly provide tools that perform actions or retrieve information, and they may also expose resources or prompts. The exact capabilities depend on what the server is designed to do.

options.text: A tool that queries an issue tracker
A new GPU driver for model training
A replacement for the model's tokenizer
A browser's CSS rendering engine

questions.text: What should be considered when exposing systems through MCP?
questions.explanation: Integrations can access sensitive data or perform actions. Servers should expose only necessary capabilities and enforce authentication, authorization, and safe input handling.

options.text: Expose every internal API to maximize usefulness
Limit capabilities and enforce permissions appropriate to the data and actions
Skip input validation because the client is an AI
Return secrets in tool responses for convenience
Disable auditing to reduce latency

questions.text: How does MCP relate to an AI agent?
questions.explanation: An agent can use MCP clients to discover and call tools exposed by MCP servers. MCP provides the connection layer; the agent provides the goal-directed decision making.

options.text: MCP can provide standardized access to tools an agent may use
MCP replaces the need for a model or agent logic

topics.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
topics.description: Learn how RAG combines retrieval with generation to ground model answers in relevant data.

lessons.title: RAG Basics
lessons.body:
# RAG Basics

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a pattern that improves model responses by retrieving relevant information and providing it as context before generation. Instead of relying only on what the model learned during training, RAG can ground answers in current or domain-specific data.

## Typical flow

1. **Prepare data**: Documents are split into chunks and indexed, often using embeddings for semantic search.
2. **Retrieve**: When a user asks a question, the system finds the most relevant chunks.
3. **Augment**: The retrieved chunks are added to the prompt or context.
4. **Generate**: The model produces an answer using both the question and retrieved context.

## Benefits and limits

RAG can reduce hallucinations and make answers more traceable to source material. It does not guarantee correctness: retrieval can miss relevant documents, return irrelevant text, or provide outdated information, so evaluation and source handling still matter.

questions.text: What is the main idea behind Retrieval-Augmented Generation?
questions.explanation: RAG retrieves relevant information and includes it in the model's context before generating a response. This helps ground the answer in external or up-to-date data.

options.text: Retrieve relevant context and use it when generating an answer
Retrain the model from scratch for every user question
Generate answers without using any input context
Store user passwords inside prompts

questions.text: Why is document chunking commonly used in RAG systems?
questions.explanation: Large documents are often split into smaller chunks so the system can retrieve the most relevant passages and fit them within context limits. Chunking also improves retrieval granularity.

options.text: To make retrieval target relevant passages and manage context size
To remove the need for indexing
To ensure the model never sees source text

questions.text: What is a limitation of RAG?
questions.explanation: RAG quality depends on retrieval quality. If relevant information is not retrieved, or if irrelevant or stale content is retrieved, the generated answer can still be wrong.

options.text: It guarantees perfect answers whenever sources exist
Poor retrieval can lead to incomplete or incorrect answers
It cannot use any domain-specific documents
It removes the need to evaluate outputs

questions.text: Which step happens before generation in a typical RAG flow?
questions.explanation: After retrieval, the system augments the prompt or context with selected passages. The model then generates a response conditioned on that context.

options.text: Retrieved context is added to the prompt or model input
The model's weights are permanently updated with the chunks
All documents are deleted to save space
The user question is discarded

questions.text: When is RAG especially useful?
questions.explanation: RAG is helpful when answers need information that is private, recent, or specific to a domain. Providing relevant source material at query time can improve usefulness and grounding.

options.text: When answers should use current or domain-specific information
When no source data exists and none is needed
When the goal is to avoid all data access
When you want the model to ignore the user question
When deterministic database transactions are the only requirement

questions.text: What does 'grounding' mean in the context of RAG?
questions.explanation: Grounding means basing a response on supplied evidence or source material. In RAG, retrieved passages provide context the model can use to produce a more supported answer.

options.text: Basing the response on relevant retrieved source material
Forcing the model to answer with only one token

topics.title: Embeddings
topics.description: Learn what embeddings are and how they represent meaning for search, clustering, and RAG.

lessons.title: Understanding Embeddings
lessons.body:
# Understanding Embeddings

An embedding is a numerical vector representation of data, such as text, images, or code. Embedding models map similar items to vectors that are close together in a high-dimensional space, which makes embeddings useful for comparing meaning.

## Common uses

- **Semantic search**: Find documents related to a query even when they do not share the same keywords.
- **Clustering**: Group similar items based on vector similarity.
- **Recommendations and retrieval**: Identify related content or candidates.
- **RAG indexing**: Store chunk embeddings so relevant passages can be retrieved for generation.

## Practical notes

Embeddings capture patterns learned by the model, but they are not perfect representations of truth or intent. The choice of embedding model, chunking strategy, and similarity metric affects retrieval quality, so systems should be evaluated on real tasks.

questions.text: What is an embedding?
questions.explanation: An embedding represents data as a vector of numbers. In many AI systems, embeddings place semantically related items near each other in vector space.

options.text: A numerical vector representation of data
A database table primary key
A human-written summary of a document
A compressed image file format

questions.text: Why are embeddings useful for semantic search?
questions.explanation: Semantic search compares the meaning of a query and documents using vector similarity. This can retrieve relevant results even when the exact query words do not appear.

options.text: They allow matching based on meaning, not only exact keywords
They guarantee the top result is always correct
They eliminate the need to store original documents

questions.text: In a RAG system, embeddings are commonly used to:
questions.explanation: RAG systems often embed document chunks and queries into vectors, then retrieve chunks with high similarity to the query. Those chunks provide context for generation.

options.text: Render the user interface
Find relevant document chunks for retrieval
Replace the need for a language model
Encrypt database backups

questions.text: What affects the quality of embedding-based retrieval?
questions.explanation: Retrieval quality depends on multiple choices, including the embedding model, how data is chunked, and how similarity is measured and evaluated. Testing on real queries is important.

options.text: Only the font used in the source documents
The embedding model, chunking, and evaluation approach
Whether the vectors are displayed as charts
The number of UI themes in the application

questions.text: If two text embeddings are close in vector space, what does that usually suggest?
questions.explanation: Embedding models are trained so that related inputs tend to have similar vectors. Closeness usually indicates semantic similarity, though results depend on the model and data.

options.text: The texts are likely similar in meaning or related
The texts have identical byte lengths
The texts were written by the same author
The texts are guaranteed to be factually true
The texts must be in the same database row

questions.text: Can embeddings be created for data other than text?
questions.explanation: Embeddings can represent many kinds of data, including images, audio, and code. Multimodal or domain-specific models learn vector representations suited to those inputs.

options.text: Yes, embeddings can represent images, audio, code, and other data
No, embeddings only work for English text

topics.title: Evaluation
topics.description: Learn how to evaluate AI systems with clear criteria, test cases, and human review where needed.

lessons.title: Evaluating AI Systems
lessons.body:
# Evaluating AI Systems

Evaluation helps you understand whether an AI system is useful, reliable, and safe for its intended task. Because model outputs can vary and fail in subtle ways, evaluation should be based on representative examples and clear criteria.

## What to evaluate

- **Quality**: Is the output correct, relevant, and complete for the task?
- **Reliability**: Does the system behave consistently across similar inputs and edge cases?
- **Safety and policy**: Does it avoid harmful, sensitive, or unauthorized behavior?
- **Cost and latency**: Is performance acceptable for the product and budget?

## Common approaches

Teams use curated test sets, automated checks, model-based graders, and human review. No single metric is enough for every case. Good evaluation combines measurable checks with judgment on real user scenarios, especially before and after changes to prompts, models, retrieval, or tools.

questions.text: Why is evaluation important for AI systems?
questions.explanation: AI outputs can be inconsistent or incorrect, so evaluation checks whether the system meets quality, safety, and product goals. It also helps detect regressions after changes.

options.text: To measure whether the system meets task and safety goals
To eliminate the need for product requirements
To guarantee users never see an error
To replace monitoring in production

questions.text: What makes a good evaluation dataset?
questions.explanation: An evaluation set should reflect the real tasks, inputs, and edge cases the system will face. Representative examples make results more meaningful than a few easy cases.

options.text: Examples that represent real use cases and important edge cases
Only cases where the current system already succeeds
Random text with no relation to the product task

questions.text: Why might human review be part of AI evaluation?
questions.explanation: Some qualities, such as helpfulness, tone, or nuanced correctness, are hard to capture with simple automated rules. Human review can judge outputs where automatic metrics are incomplete.

options.text: Because humans can train the model during every evaluation run
Because some output qualities require judgment beyond simple automated checks
Because automated tests are never useful
Because evaluation should avoid clear criteria

questions.text: When should you re-run evaluations?
questions.explanation: Changes to prompts, models, retrieval, tools, or data can affect behavior. Re-evaluating after changes helps catch regressions and confirm improvements.

options.text: After relevant changes such as prompts, models, or retrieval logic
Only once, before the first prototype
Never, if the demo looked good
Only when changing the website colors

questions.text: What is a regression in the context of AI system changes?
questions.explanation: A regression is when a change makes behavior worse on cases that previously worked or mattered. Evaluations help detect regressions before they reach users.

options.text: A decline in behavior or quality after a change
An improvement in latency
A new feature request from users
A database backup process
A larger context window

questions.text: Is one metric usually enough to evaluate an AI feature?
questions.explanation: AI features often involve tradeoffs among correctness, usefulness, safety, latency, and cost. A combination of checks gives a more complete view than a single metric.

options.text: No, multiple criteria are often needed for a complete picture
Yes, one accuracy number is always sufficient

topics.title: Deployment
topics.description: Learn practical concerns for deploying AI features, including reliability, monitoring, and safety controls.

lessons.title: Deploying AI Features
lessons.body:
# Deploying AI Features

Deploying an AI feature means making it available to users in a way that is reliable, observable, and safe. Production AI systems need more than a working prompt: they need controls around inputs, outputs, failures, and change management.

## Key concerns

- **Configuration**: Manage model settings, API keys, endpoints, and feature flags through environment/configuration, not hardcoded secrets.
- **Reliability**: Handle timeouts, rate limits, retries, and fallback behavior when model providers or tools fail.
- **Monitoring**: Track latency, errors, cost, and quality signals so issues are visible after release.
- **Safety**: Validate inputs, constrain tool permissions, and review outputs where mistakes could cause harm.

## Rollout

Gradual rollouts, evaluations, and clear ownership help teams ship AI changes safely. Because behavior can change with prompts, models, or data, deployment should include a plan for observing and improving the system over time.

questions.text: Where should API keys and model endpoints be managed in production?
questions.explanation: Secrets and environment-specific settings should come from configuration such as environment variables or secret managers. Hardcoding them in source code risks leaks and makes environments harder to manage.

options.text: In environment/configuration management, not hardcoded in source
Committed directly into the frontend bundle
Inside public issue comments
As plain text in user-visible error messages

questions.text: Why is monitoring important after deploying an AI feature?
questions.explanation: Monitoring helps teams detect failures, latency spikes, cost changes, and quality issues in real usage. AI behavior can drift or fail in cases not seen during development.

options.text: To detect errors, performance issues, and quality problems in production
To avoid having any tests before release
To make model outputs always deterministic

questions.text: What is a good way to handle provider timeouts or rate limits?
questions.explanation: Production systems should anticipate external failures with bounded retries, timeouts, and fallback behavior. This improves reliability and gives users a clearer failure path.

options.text: Retry forever without limits
Use timeouts and bounded error handling or fallback behavior
Expose raw provider credentials to the client so it can retry
Ignore the failure and return a success response

questions.text: Why can gradual rollout be useful for AI features?
questions.explanation: A gradual rollout limits the impact of unexpected behavior and gives teams time to observe metrics and user feedback. It is especially helpful when model behavior is hard to predict fully before release.

options.text: It reduces risk by exposing changes to a limited audience first
It guarantees no evaluation is needed
It prevents the need for logging
It makes prompts impossible to change later

questions.text: Which practice improves safety for AI features that can trigger actions?
questions.explanation: Actions should be constrained by permissions and validated before execution. Least privilege and guardrails reduce the damage from incorrect model decisions or malicious inputs.

options.text: Validate inputs and limit tool permissions to what is needed
Allow every tool to run with administrator access
Skip authorization checks for faster responses
Trust model output as a security boundary
Log secrets so actions can be replayed

questions.text: Should deployment planning include cost considerations for AI features?
questions.explanation: Model calls, retrieval, and tool usage can create ongoing costs that vary with traffic and prompt size. Tracking and designing for cost helps keep the feature sustainable.

options.text: Yes, usage-based model and infrastructure costs should be considered
No, AI feature costs are always fixed and negligible
